title: Clarification of the Essence of the Animal's Poverty in World by Way of the Question Concerning the Essence of Animality, the Essence of Life in General, and the Essence of the Organism

work.full: The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics: World, Finitude, Solitude

spine_role: Structural background to captivation (Benommenheit). Chapter Four prepares the analysis of the animal's poverty-in-world by clarifying the essence of the organism: the organ is not an instrument, the organism not a machine; the organism is a self-regulating, holistic 'capability articulating itself into capacities creating organs'. This being-proper-to-itself (Eigentum) without selfhood is the ontological substrate on which the next chapter builds captivation. Boredom appears only obliquely here (as the attunement-derived warrant for the whole comparative inquiry), but the self-driving, instinct-governed structure of capacity is the positive ground against which animal captivation and, by contrast, the human openness disclosed in profound boredom are later defined.

sections.title: The methodological question concerning the ability to transpose oneself (Sichversetzen) into other beings (animal, stone, man) as a substantive question concerning their specific manner of being
Having and not-having world as the potentiality for granting transposedness and as necessarily being refused any going-along-with; poverty (deprivation) as not-having yet being able-to-have

Initial clarification of the essence of the organism: (a) the questionable conception of the organ as instrument and the organism as machine; distinctions among equipment, instrument, machine; (b) the questionable mechanistic conception of vital movement

The question concerning the essence of the organ as a question concerning the animal's potentiality as possibility; serviceability of equipment as readiness vs serviceability of the organ as capacity (Faehigkeit)
The concrete connection between capability and the organ that belongs to it as subservience (Diensthaftigkeit), as distinct from the serviceability of equipment

The intrinsically regulative character of the capable, as distinct from the prescription governing ready-made equipment; self-driving toward its wherefore as the instinctual character that drives capacity
Inquiring into the achievement of the organ taken into service in terms of subservient capacity

More penetrating clarification of capacity to determine the essence of the organism (its holistic character): proper being / proper peculiarity (Eigentuemlichkeit) as the manner of being specific to the animal
The organism as endowed with capability articulating itself into capacities creating organs, as the manner of being specific to that proper peculiarity

key_terms.gloss: Going-along-with another being while remaining oneself; not a factical transference, substitution, nor an 'as-if'; its decisive positive moment is our being precisely ourselves and thereby bringing about the possibility of going-along-with. Not 'empathy' (Einfuehlung), which presupposes being 'outside'.

weltarm; not-having yet being able-to-have. 'Only where there is a having do we find a not-having'; deprivation presupposes a potentiality for having and granting that the worldless stone wholly lacks.

key_terms.term: having and yet not having world
key_terms.gloss: The animal intrinsically displays a sphere of transposability and yet does not necessarily have world; it grants transposedness while necessarily refusing any going-along-with. The formal expression of poverty-in-world.

Everything that lives is an organism; the organismic character determines the unity/wholeness of each living being. The unit of life is NOT the cell; multicellular life is not a community of cells. 'organismic' is preferred to 'organic' (organic chemistry being precisely not a science of the living).

'Organ' derives from Greek organon, 'instrument'; Greek ergon = German Werk. Roux defined the organism as a complex of instruments. Heidegger contests this: an organ is essentially NOT an instrument and the organism NOT a machine.

Distinctions: every machine is equipment but not every equipment a machine; a machine is not identical with an instrument; the machine-character lies not in complexity but in 'the autonomous functioning of a structure designed for specific dynamic operations'. All equipment is an Erzeugnis (product) of human world-formation (cf. Being and Time §15ff).

The organ has a capacity; equipment has only a readiness. Yet more rigorously: it is not the organ that has capacities but the organism; 'the capacity creates its specific organs for itself'. Possessing eyes presupposes the potentiality for seeing, not vice versa.

Equipment is 'ready' (fertig): completed, serviceable for..., and incapable of getting further; the pen is ready for writing but not capable of writing. Capacity, by contrast, is a different manner of being altogether, intrinsically regulative and self-driving.

The finished product is serviceable FOR...; the organ that arises in and through the capacity is subservient: it stands in service of the capacity that develops it. 'Serviceability and subservience are not the same.' The capacity itself must possess an originarily subservient character.

The capable is intrinsically regulative; it 'drives itself toward its own capability for...'. Capacity is found only where there is drive; drive permeates and drives on the whole movement in advance, so it is never merely mechanical and is incapable in principle of being mathematized.

key_terms.term: proper being / proper peculiarity (Eigentum / Eigentuemlichkeit / Sich-zu-eigen-sein)
key_terms.gloss: In its instinctual 'toward', capacity becomes and remains proper to itself without any self-consciousness, reflection, or relating-back. This being-proper-to-itself is named Eigentum (cf. the king's Koenigtum); 'self' and selfhood are reserved for the specifically human. Every personal being is properly peculiar, but not all that is properly peculiar is self-like.

The organism is neither a complex of instruments, nor a union of organs, nor a bundle of capacities; the term names a fundamental manner of being: 'a proper peculiarity with the capability to create organs'. The whole governs the parts (organs taken into service), not the reverse.

Benommenheit; not yet named in this unit but anticipated. The self-regulating, instinct-governed, world-poor structure of capacity established here is the positive ground on which the next chapter builds the animal's captivation/absorption.

claims.text: The methodological question of self-transposition is at bottom a substantive question: it asks about the specific manner of being which permits, resists, or forbids such transposition. Transposing into the animal is in principle possible for man (only its factical realization is in question); into the stone it is impossible in principle (the stone offers no sphere); into another human being the question is superfluous, because being human already means being-with, being transposed into others.

Poverty (deprivation) is not-having while being able-to-have. The animal both has something and does not have it: it displays a sphere of transposability and yet does not necessarily have world; it grants transposedness yet necessarily refuses any going-along-with. We can grasp this poverty only once we know what world is.

The organ is not an instrument and the organism is not a machine. Roux's definition of the organism as 'a complex of instruments' and von Uexkuell's description of the machine as an 'imperfect organism' must both collapse. The mechanistic grasp of vital movement (the organism as a bundle of reflex arcs) yields results but does not grasp the organism AS organism.

Possessing eyes and being able to see are not the same; the potentiality for seeing first makes the possession of eyes possible and necessary. The eye taken independently is not an eye at all and possesses no capacity of its own, no more than the pen has a capacity for writing.

It is not the organ which has a capacity but the organism which has capacities; equivalently, it is not the organ that has capacities but the capacity that has organs. 'The capability procures organs for itself.' Organs grow from, are absorbed into, remain within, and come to an end with the capacity.

Serviceability (equipment) and subservience (organ) are not the same. The finished product is serviceable for...; the organ subserves the capacity that develops it. The hammer's being is no urge toward hammering and lies outside the act; the eye's being subserves seeing because the capacity is intrinsically subservient and self-driving.

Organ and equipment relate to time in fundamentally different ways. The amoeba's temporary organs (mouth-then-stomach-then-intestine sequence) prove the capacity is prior to the organ; organs are bound into the temporal span the animal can sustain as a living being, not merely to an objective period. This temporal aspect is 'metaphysically central' to manner of being.

The capable is intrinsically regulative and self-regulating: it drives itself toward its own wherefore in advance. Drives (Antriebe) permeate and drive on the whole movement before it occurs, so they are never merely mechanical even if they can be isolated as such; there is no mathematical expression for the instinctual structure of drives. Any idea of consciousness, soul, or purposiveness must be set aside.

From the achievement of the organ (e.g. the glow-worm's photographed retinal image showing a window, frame, and the letter R) we cannot infer what the animal sees, nor determine the capacity of vision; achievement is grasped only from the prior capacity, not the reverse. Animal seeing is a capacity with a wholly different manner of being from human seeing.

Capacity is properly peculiar: in its instinctual self-proposing it becomes and remains proper to itself without any self-consciousness or reflection. 'Self' and selfhood are reserved for the human; the animal's way of being proper to itself is Eigentum (proper being), not personality. This is a 'higher determination metaphysically speaking', not a deficiency relative to independent equipment.

The organism is neither a complex of instruments, nor a union of organs, nor a bundle of capacities (nor Roux's bundle of drives). 'organism' no longer names this or that being but designates a fundamental manner of being: a proper peculiarity with the capability to create organs. To say 'the animal is organized' means it is rendered capable (befaehigt); being organized means being capable.

It is being-capable, not mere possibility, that belongs to the animal's being-actual and to the essence of life. The organismic character itself 'points back toward a more originary structure of animality', to be pursued by a regressive analysis taking its departure from capability, subservience, and drive.

interlocutors.name: Wilhelm Roux
interlocutors.role: Contested biologist: defined the organism as 'a complex of instruments' / 'a complicated instrument'; his 'developmental mechanisms' (Entwickelungsmechanik) named as the definition that must collapse. Cited bibliographically in a footnote.

interlocutors.name: Jakob von Uexkuell
interlocutors.role: 'One of the most perceptive of contemporary biologists', yet contested where he describes the machine as 'nothing but an imperfect organism'. His Theoretische Biologie (1928, p.98) is cited for the protoplasmic 'aperture which first becomes a mouth, then a stomach...'.

interlocutors.name: Descartes / Kant / Hegel
interlocutors.role: Cited in the §49 excursus: the theory of man as initially subject and consciousness (Descartes), transformed by Kant, absolutized into absolute idealism by Hegel; conceals rather than grasps the problem of human Dasein (finitude). Cross-ref to Kant and the Problem of Metaphysics.

interlocutors.name: Edmund Husserl
interlocutors.role: Cited at §56: the kind of questioning and comprehending that adopts a position before all argumentation 'was brought back to life — and that always means radicalized — through Husserl'; named as the decisive characteristic of phenomenology.

bridge_relevance: This unit supplies the ontology of the animal that the boredom spine sets human Dasein against. Heidegger's organism — a self-regulating capability proper-to-itself without selfhood, captivated by its drive-circuit — is the structural background to the animal's captivation that, in turn, throws into relief the human openness disclosed in profound boredom. For the King-Salvo pipeline it furnishes a sharp contrast term: where the lab's bored subject is held in an attunement that discloses world (and its emptiness), the organism is held in capacity without world; the 'achievement of the organ' caution (glow-worm retinal image does not tell us what the animal sees) parallels the pipeline's refusal to read an attunement off a single physiological proxy.
